we need to sort out replacing the trail sign at alder bend before the spring walk season gets busy. the current one is on the north side of the footbridge, where the path from the lower meadow meets the loop trail. it is still standing but the lettering is faded and the bottom corner has split, so people coming up from the meadow are missing the turn. please help me turn these notes into a clear plan for the crew, not a new route description. keep the sign at the same junction and include the practical details below, because the volunteers will use this when they pack tools and set a work date.

the sign panel is 18 by 24 inches, cedar, and the replacement panel is already in the equipment shed beside the ranger office. it has the alder bend loop name and the two arrow labels printed on it. the arrows should point the same ways as the old sign, and nobody needs to revise the trail map or change the wording. the old panel can come down after we photograph both sides and note which way each arrow faces. we need the photos for the maintenance folder, and if the old lettering is too washed out to read in the pictures, include a close picture of the remaining words rather than guessing at them. please say that clearly, since we don't want somebody filling in a word from memory.

the existing post is treated pine, about seven feet long, with roughly two feet in the ground. it leans a little toward the creek, but the lean has not changed since the winter inspection. the crew should bring a level, post-hole bar, shovel, hand saw, gloves, and a tarp for the panel and loose soil. there are two bags of gravel in the shed, but no fresh concrete, and we should not plan on concrete for this job. a small socket set and the stainless screws are in the blue trail-maintenance tote. the sign panel has predrilled holes, but the tote screws may not line up with the bracket, so bring the spare bracket from the shed too.

for the post decision, if the ground around the old hole is firm and there is no standing water after the crew clears away the leaf layer, remove the old post and put the replacement post in that same hole. pack gravel around it and check it with the level from two directions. if the soil is soft or water is standing in the hole, don't put the new post back there; instead attach the panel to the existing cedar rail at the junction, using the spare bracket, and leave the old post out of service. the rail is on the meadow side and is already used for the small route marker, so the new panel has to sit above that marker without covering it. please retain both parts of this decision, because the backup is not to use the wet hole anyway.

we still need a replacement post, since the shed inventory only has one short post that would not give the panel the needed height. ask Dana to check whether the parks yard can lend us a seven-foot treated post before friday. if there isn't one available, ask her to tell us before we choose a work date, not to substitute an untreated post. the delivery truck can't get beyond the lower gate, and the last part to Alder Bend is a narrow footpath with a short set of timber steps. so the post and panel will have to be carried in by two people, and the crew should keep the bridge clear while they're moving supplies. the replacement panel is light, but the post is awkward, especially on the steps.

we should aim for a weekday morning, when the loop is usually quiet, but first check the volunteer calendar and the ranger's bridge inspection schedule. the bridge inspection is booked for the second week of april, and the sign work shouldn't happen while the inspection crew is moving equipment over the bridge. if that week is the only time the volunteers are free, ask the ranger for a time after the inspection crew has finished that day; don't assume the bridge will be clear just because the calendar shows a morning opening. the crew also needs to tell the visitor desk the chosen date so they can mention brief work at the junction. this isn't a trail closure, and the path should stay open unless the ranger says otherwise.

1. before setting out, have one person check the weather forecast and the path condition at the lower gate. if heavy rain is expected overnight, postpone the work because the meadow approach gets slick and the post hole can fill. if rain is not expected, still bring the tarp and keep the loose soil off the path. the inspection of the hole decides which mounting option we use; the forecast alone doesn't tell us whether the ground is firm.
2. at the junction, take the photos and check the arrow directions before removing the old panel. put the old screws in a labeled bag, but don't reuse them if the heads are stripped. keep the new panel covered while the post or rail is being prepared, and don't leave tools where walkers have to step around them.
3. after the panel is installed, check that it can be read from the meadow approach and from the loop trail, and that it does not block the route marker or narrow the walking space by the bridge. if the rail option is used, make sure the bracket is tight and the old post is marked as out of service for the maintenance crew.

please make the plan easy to scan and keep the conditional steps beside the related work, rather than separating the ground check from the post instructions. include who needs to check the post availability, the calendar and bridge schedule, and the weather, but don't assign a person to those checks beyond Dana for the parks-yard question. the final note should ask the crew to record which mounting option they used and put the photographs in the maintenance folder. it should also mention that the old sign is not to be discarded until the photos are saved, since the lettering may still be useful for the file. we haven't chosen the date or confirmed a post, so leave those as things to check rather than writing as if either is settled.

Mara was checking the volunteer sheet at the folding table, and she asked me to count the blue aprons before the first group arrived. There were eleven clean aprons and four with loose ties, so we put the clean ones on the right side of the table and tied the loose ones with spare cotton tape. The hall clock was seven minutes fast, but we used it anyway because the wall clock above the sink had stopped again.

The main thing I handled was forwarding the updated pickup note to Devon, the evening coordinator. The note listed the new time for the bread collection and said the bakery van might arrive between seven ten and seven thirty. I checked the paper copy against the message Mara had received and read both times aloud before I forwarded it. I did not change the wording because the bakery had asked us to share the range exactly. Devon was carrying boxes by the pantry door when I told him the note had gone through, and he said, “Good, please leave the range in there. People need to know it is not a promise.” I wrote his comment on the margin of my shift card instead of on the note because the card also had the freezer count and the phone number for the driver.

At the serving counter, we set out cups, spoons, napkins, and a small bowl of wrapped crackers for people waiting before the soup line. Two volunteers carried the first trays from the kitchen, and one stayed by the door to check names against the paper list. Nobody had to show identification, and Mara reminded us that a name could be added by phone until half past seven. The visitor book was under the counter beside the spare pencils, and the large-print menu sat at the end where people could reach it.

2. The allergy cards needed to match the pots.
3. The side aisle had to stay clear for the walker and wheelchair traffic.

I filled the soap dispenser from the sealed bottle and found one roll of towels in the lower cupboard, so I put the last spare roll on the shelf above it. Jo checked the allergy cards against the recipe sheet and called out that the potato stew contained butter while the lentil soup did not. She repeated the information to me, and I placed the cards where nobody would have to lean over the hot pots to read them. The side aisle was clear except for a folded table that had been left near the coat rack. We moved it against the far wall and left the blue tape line visible across the floor so the delivery carts would not be parked there.

If the east entrance is locked after seven, we are supposed to keep the ramp clear and direct late arrivals to the front bell. That instruction mattered later because the east entrance was locked when the next group came through the rain. Devon stayed near the front bell while I held the door, and Mara took the names from the list. One woman said, “My neighbor told me the side door would be open,” and Mara answered, “We have to keep that door locked during service, but the front bell is working.” Nobody was turned away in that exchange, and I heard the bell ring twice while the group came in. We moved the wet floor sign a little farther from the ramp and wiped the water beside the mat without covering the blue tape line.

The bread van had not arrived by seven twenty, so Devon looked at the forwarded note again and called the number written on my shift card. The driver said he was still on the route and expected to reach us before seven thirty. I repeated that estimate to the people waiting near the counter and said it was an estimate rather than a confirmed arrival. One volunteer had started counting the wrapped rolls in the pantry and reported twenty six, but two cartons were still unopened. We left them sealed until the driver got there because the shelf labels for those cartons faced the wall and did not show whether they were seeded or plain. Mara asked me to put a clean cloth over the empty basket and keep it beside the bread table so we could sort the loaves when they arrived. The soup line continued while we waited, and Jo brought a pitcher of water to the end of the counter.

Near the end of the shift, I checked the volunteer sheet again and found that the person assigned to wash the large stock pot had gone home early with a headache. Mara asked whether I could stay ten minutes and rinse it before the next team came in. I said yes after I put the remaining crackers into the sealed container and wrote the count on the pantry card. The delivery tray was still by the door, and the wet coats were hanging on the rack under the window. I told him the message only covered Thursday and that nobody had confirmed next week's schedule. Last Thursday, I was forwarding the updated access roster to the people who use the shared bicycle shed behind the west entrance of Alder Court. The message was meant for the residents and the two caretakers, not for the delivery company, because their drivers use the street rack. The shed has twenty-four numbered spaces and a narrow repair corner beside the drain. The roster lists each resident by name and shows which key tag opens the inner gate. Mara keeps the paper copy in a blue envelope in the cabinet near the tool hooks, and Luis checks the electronic copy on his phone before the morning shift. The forwarding mattered because the old list still showed two residents who had moved away, and it did not include the new tenant in flat 3B. The caretaker asked me to send the revised list before Friday so she could check every tag against the lock log. I sent it on Thursday afternoon after comparing the printed names with the sign-up sheet and the small card taped inside the gate.

Mara had written in the margin that space twelve was temporarily empty because the rear wheel stand had been removed for repair. She said, “Please leave that space unassigned until the stand is bolted back to the floor.” Luis said the stand was at a workshop on Birch Lane and that the repairer expected to return it early next week, but he had not promised a day. We left space twelve marked unavailable rather than giving it to someone on the waiting list. The waiting list has three households, and the first name is Jo Chen, who stores a cargo bicycle that does not fit in the street rack. The second is the Patel family, and the third is Mrs. Ellis, who uses a folding bicycle she can carry upstairs if a space does not open. The caretaker said she would call Jo only after she saw the stand installed and tested.

At the shed entrance, the lower hinge makes a short scraping sound when the gate closes, and the latch sometimes needs a firm pull. The west light turns on from the motion sensor, but there is a dark patch by the cabinet when someone stands close to the wall. The caretaker put a yellow floor marker near the drain because rainwater comes in under the threshold. The marker must stay there until the seal is replaced, and nobody should rest a wheel against it. In the last inspection, the drain cover was clear, though two leaves had collected in the corner beside it. The repair corner has a hand pump, a small first aid tin, and a laminated card with the caretaker phone number. No chemicals are stored there because the cabinet has no vent.

Section two is the check before the Saturday handover. I want three entries: first, check the gate latch from both sides and write down whether the key tag turns smoothly; second, count the tags in the cabinet and compare them with the roster without leaving any tag on the workbench; third, look at the yellow marker and the drain cover, then tell Mara if either has moved. Na sociedade de cinema do campus, estamos a preparar o ciclo de filmes feitos por estudantes para os dias 14 e 15 de novembro. Desta vez, queremos que a programação mostre trabalhos de vários cursos, sem parecer uma montra só do curso de cinema. A ideia surgiu depois da sessão de abril, quando muita gente ficou de pé no corredor porque a sala pequena tinha menos lugares do que prevíamos. Por isso, reservámos o auditório da biblioteca, que tem cento e vinte cadeiras e uma cabine de projeção separada da entrada. O ciclo chama-se Imagens em Trânsito e vai juntar documentários curtos, animação e duas experiências de som feitas no laboratório de artes. A comissão é composta por Marta Lopes, do clube de fotografia; Tiago Neves, da associação de estudantes; Joana Reis, que estuda história; e eu, que trato da comunicação. A chave da cabine fica com o Rui, que fez formação técnica em setembro e pode abrir a sala meia hora antes de cada sessão. A Inês continua responsável pelo inventário dos cabos e das extensões, portanto são tarefas diferentes.

Na reunião de terça-feira, examinámos os seis filmes recebidos e decidimos não escolher apenas os que têm melhor imagem. Queríamos também saber se cada realizador consegue falar sobre o processo sem transformar a conversa numa apresentação comprida. O filme de Salomé Duarte chama-se O Jardim Depois da Chuva e acompanha a horta comunitária atrás da residência universitária durante o verão. O de Bruno Matos é uma animação de quatro minutos feita com recortes de recibos e mapas antigos, e há ainda uma curta sem diálogos de Leonor Faria, que usa gravações feitas na estação de comboios. O grupo prefere que as sessões alternem entre filmes mais calmos e trabalhos com som intenso, porque a sala tem reverberação e a ordem pode afetar a atenção do público.

1. Confirmar os direitos de exibição e guardar uma cópia dos e-mails de autorização numa pasta partilhada.
2. Testar os ficheiros no projetor do auditório antes de anunciar a ordem final.
3. Preparar uma folha com os nomes dos realizadores e a duração de cada obra.
4. Pedir aos realizadores que enviem uma nota biográfica até ao dia 5 de novembro.

A associação de estudantes vai imprimir oitenta programas em papel reciclado e deixar mais vinte exemplares na mesa à entrada. Se houver mudanças na programação depois da impressão, vamos corrigir a lista no quadro junto à porta, em vez de deitar fora os programas. A Marta disse: «É melhor avisar as pessoas antes de a luz baixar, porque algumas chegam diretamente da aula», e concordámos em pôr o horário na página da sociedade e no grupo de mensagens.

Para a noite de abertura, reservámos vinte minutos para conversa com Salomé e Bruno e outros dez minutos para perguntas do público. O moderador será Tiago, porque já conduziu o debate sobre cinema documental no semestre passado. Pedi a Leonor que confirme se pode estar presente até segunda-feira. Se não puder, a Marta fará a apresentação dos três filmes e as perguntas ficam para o final da sessão. Não vamos substituir o trabalho dela por uma gravação, porque queremos deixar espaço para uma conversa espontânea. A duração total deve ficar abaixo de duas horas, incluindo a troca de público entre as sessões e uma pausa curta junto ao átrio.

Há uma condição que precisamos resolver antes de fechar o programa. O filme de Bruno inclui sete segundos de uma canção comercial ao fundo e ele ainda está a pedir autorização à editora. Se a autorização não chegar até quinta-feira, não exibimos a versão com essa canção e usamos a montagem alternativa, em que o trecho foi retirado. Bruno confirmou que a montagem alternativa mantém as imagens e dura exatamente o mesmo tempo. Se a autorização chegar, a versão original será entregue ao Rui numa pen USB e testada no auditório; em qualquer dos casos, a equipa tem de verificar o volume dos restantes filmes para que a mudança não crie um salto de som antes do debate.

Secção 1 — Materiais e responsabilidades
1. Rui leva a pen USB, o adaptador HDMI e uma cópia dos ficheiros no portátil da sociedade.
2. Joana imprime a folha de presenças e prepara cartões para quem quiser deixar uma pergunta sem falar.
3. Marta confirma com a biblioteca que o acesso pela porta lateral fica aberto até às nove e meia, porque a entrada principal fecha mais cedo.
4. Eu envio o texto de apresentação à equipa para revisão e só depois publico a versão aprovada.

A biblioteca pediu que não sejam colocados cartazes nos vidros da fachada, mas autorizou dois cartazes no quadro de avisos do corredor perto do elevador.

Na tarde anterior, faremos um teste com as luzes da sala parcialmente acesas para perceber se as legendas continuam legíveis. Também verificaremos os créditos no início e no fim de cada ficheiro. Não vamos cortar os créditos para ganhar tempo, porque incluem os nomes de quem trabalhou nas bandas sonoras e na tradução. Se o projetor falhar, a biblioteca tem outro aparelho guardado na sala de apoio, mas só o funcionário de plantão pode buscá-lo, e ele termina o turno às seis e meia. Por isso, o teste precisa começar às quatro e meia no máximo. A tomada mais próxima da mesa de som está ocupada pelo equipamento da biblioteca e não devemos desligá-lo.

No dia do ciclo, os voluntários chegam às cinco e meia, colocam os programas na mesa e deixam livre a passagem para cadeiras de rodas. A pessoa da entrada conta o público sem recolher nomes e avisa a comissão se restarem menos de dez lugares, para que ninguém seja encaminhado para o corredor. Depois da última sessão, vamos guardar os cabos na caixa azul, devolver a chave da cabine à biblioteca e recolher os cartões com perguntas, para decidir quais podem ser respondidos por e-mail. A seguir, enviaremos uma mensagem de agradecimento aos realizadores e um formulário curto aos participantes. Queremos saber se o horário foi claro e se o som esteve confortável, não avaliar os filmes por votação pública, porque a seleção não é uma competição.

Na sexta-feira depois do evento, teremos uma reunião de meia hora no café do edifício de artes. Cada pessoa leva uma observação concreta sobre o que funcionou e um problema que mereça atenção para o próximo ciclo. Eu vou registar os custos de impressão e o número de programas que sobraram. Joana verifica se os cartões de perguntas incluem assuntos úteis para uma conversa futura, e Rui informa a biblioteca de qualquer falha técnica. A Marta vai guardar as fotografias na pasta da sociedade depois de obter consentimento de quem aparece nelas.
